While most Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ: RIVN) investors and observers are focusing on the company's vehicle deliveries and adoption into the mainstream, the company's most valuable bet might actually be in robotics.

In 2025, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe founded Mind Robotics, an AI-enabled technology company focused on building high-impact robots. The electric vehicle company owns about a third of Mind, and in turn, Mind serves as Rivian's primary manufacturing partner.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Mind hired an experienced executive this week, Doug Field. Field previously ran Tesla's Model 3 program and Ford Motor Company's EV operations. He will serve as president of Mind Robotics. The start-up's partnership with Rivian gives it a leg up on competition and an immediate place to deploy its technology.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Mind Robotics could have extensive use cases across manufacturing. Rivian's stake is reportedly worth a little more than $1 billion at this point. If the business takes off, Rivian and its investors will be along for the ride. Mind is also well-funded for an early-stage company, having reported raising $1 billion in the past year.

Rivian launched its more affordable R2 fleet this year and delivered a record 19,248 vehicles in the third fiscal quarter. Shares of Rivian are still down 34% this year and more than 87% for all time as of this writing. Ultimately, Rivian still needs its EV lineup to become profitable, but the surprise success of Mind Robotics could be a lucrative win for investors.

Tesla trades at 369 times earnings with negative free cash flow, while Alphabet's Waymo runs driverless rides backed by a profitable parent company.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Tesla didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat TSLA. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

On October 16, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the class certification orders in LoSavio v. Tesla (No. 25-7927). The suit claims Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) falsely advertised that cars sold since October 2016 had the hardware needed for full self-driving.

24/7 Wall St.

Circuit Judges Ronald Gould, Jay Bybee and Daniel Bress sent the case back to US District Judge Rita Lin, who had certified three classes of California buyers. Class status turns thousands of small claims into one large liability, so losing it cuts Tesla's exposure in this case.

The stock fell anyway, closing at $354.72, down 2.13% in a move that tracked a broader tech selloff rather than the ruling. For a company valued at $1.40 trillion, the open question is whether self-driving software and robotaxis deliver the revenue that valuation assumes.

TSLA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
What the Ninth Circuit Actually Decided

The panel found that individual questions about what each buyer saw before purchase made class treatment inappropriate. The challenged statement sat on Tesla's Autopilot page. Buyers did not have to visit that page to complete a purchase, so plaintiffs could not show every class member was exposed to it.

The order reversed two damages classes and one injunctive-relief class. The ruling addresses class status only; the court made no finding on whether Tesla's hardware claims were true, and the case continues before Judge Lin.

title: History Says Tesla Stock Swings Hard on Earnings. It Has Moved 8% or More After 10 of Its Last 15 Reports.
detail:
History Says Tesla Stock Swings Hard on Earnings. It Has Moved 8% or More After 10 of Its Last 15 Reports.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 3:49 AM CDT 5 min read
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) will post its third-quarter numbers after the market close on Wednesday, Oct. 21. And if the past few years are any guide, shareholders could see a big move the next day.

Since the start of 2023, the electric-car maker has put out 15 quarterly reports. Measured from the close on report day to the close a trading day later, the stock moved 8% or more after 10 of them.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The average move, up or down, was about 9%. With shares trading around $368 as of this writing, a 9% move would be about $33 a share.

The moves have tilted one way, too. Tesla stock dropped after nine of the 15 reports, including each of the past three.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Big moves, mainly down

After an 11% pop following its January 2023 report, shares dropped between 9% and 10% after each of the next three.

Showing what Tesla's price cuts in early 2023 did to its profitability, the company's operating margin narrowed from 16% in the fourth quarter of 2022 to 11.4% three months later. It then kept dropping to 9.6% the next quarter and 7.6% the quarter after that. Each report showed a lower margin than the one before it. And each pushed shares down around 9% or more.

Then 2024 swung both ways: down 12% after the January report, up 12% in April, down 12% in July, and up 22% in October -- the largest move of the whole stretch.

The 2025 reports were quieter with just July's 8% fall clearing the bar. And this year, the January and April reports each brought losses of around 3.5% before July's 14.5% drop.

What caused the big moves?

The common thread in the big moves is operating income, or the profit Tesla's business makes before interest and taxes. All seven big declines followed a quarter in which operating income fell year over year.

That includes January 2024, when operating income sank 47% and Tesla warned that its vehicle volume growth rate in 2024 "may be notably lower" than in 2023. It also includes July 2024, when operating income fell 33%, and this July, when it fell 57%.

On the flip side, two of the three big gains followed a jump in operating income. It grew 49% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2022. Even more, in the third quarter of 2024, it rose 54% as Tesla's operating margin widened to 10.8% from 6.3% the quarter before. That report led to the 22% gain.

There's always a second chance in the stock market. Investors who missed out on Apple and Amazon in the early 2000s had access to picks like Tesla and Nvidia in the 2010s. Even in this past decade, stocks like Palantir minted new millionaires.

Micron (NASDAQ: MU) and Sandisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) have built substantial wealth for early investors over the past year. Opportunities like these will exist in the 2030s and beyond, but there's one growth stock that looks attractive right now and is riding the same tailwinds as the memory chipmakers. Here's why Penguin Solutions (NASDAQ: PENG) is worth monitoring.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
This memory play is growing faster than people realize

The front-line number, 68% year-over-year revenue growth in the company's fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, is impressive. However, the metrics are actually more compelling if you look at the company's key growth segment.

Penguin Solutions reports three segments each quarter: advanced computing, integrated memory, and optimized LED. Integrated memory is the most important segment, since it includes key memory products for AI data centers. Its DRAM modules are the top seller, while Penguin Solutions' CXL memory modules are surging in demand as a recognized solution to the memory wall bottleneck.

CXL enables GPUs to access a memory pool. Without this setup, a single AI chip can crash or slow down an AI model if it runs out of memory. Since CXL solves this problem and Penguin Solutions is one of the few companies already delivering this technology, it has a massive tailwind.

These trends helped Penguin Solutions' integrated memory segment grow by 158% year over year. It grew much faster than the other two segments and made up 60% of overall sales. As the memory segment grows and accounts for a larger share of total revenue, Penguin Solutions' revenue and net income growth rates should continue to accelerate.

Penguin Solutions is winning more customers

While consumer-facing companies like Walmart must consistently win over many customers, Penguin Solutions only needs a handful to generate substantial revenue growth. That's why it was such a big deal when the company won six new AI infrastructure data center customers in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.

That customer profile included four neocloud providers, which must aggressively scale out data centers to deliver for customers. The data center scale-out will increase demand for Penguin Solutions' memory products, especially its CXL products that address the memory wall.

title: BYD or Tesla: Which Is a Better Stock?

BYD or Tesla: Which Is a Better Stock?
Lawrence Nga, The Motley Fool

At first glance, this looks like an easy comparison.

Both sell electric vehicles. Both have ambitious plans for the future. Both have turned themselves into global brands.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But here's the interesting part. Investors aren't really choosing between two EV companies anymore. BYD Company (OTC: BYDDY) is quietly building something that looks increasingly like a global manufacturing powerhouse, while Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) is asking investors to look far beyond cars.

So which one offers the more compelling investment case today? The answer starts with understanding what you're actually buying.

Image source: Getty Images.
BYD is building a global business

The BYD investment case is relatively straightforward.

The company has built an enormous manufacturing scale in China, developed deep expertise in batteries and electric vehicles, and integrated much of its supply chain. Now it is taking that formula overseas.

The shift is already visible in the numbers. In the first half of 2026, BYD generated 181.3 billion renminbi of revenue from overseas markets, compared with RMB163.5 billion from China. International revenue, therefore, accounted for roughly 53% of total revenue.

And the momentum is accelerating. In August, BYD sold 440,293 new-energy vehicles, up 17.8% year over year. Overseas shipments surged 134.5% to 189,466, while domestic sales declined 14.3%.

That matters because China's EV market is becoming increasingly competitive. BYD's first-half revenue fell 7.1%, while net profit attributable to shareholders dropped 20.5%.

The long-term question is therefore not whether BYD can sell more cars. It clearly can. The question is whether it can leverage its cost advantages, manufacturing expertise, and battery technology worldwide -- and earn attractive returns while doing so.

That is a difficult execution challenge. But it is also a relatively tangible one. BYD is already building factories and distribution networks across international markets. For instance, its first passenger-vehicle factory in Hungary is moving toward production, while the company plans to expand its manufacturing footprint over time.

If BYD succeeds, it could become far less dependent on China's fiercely competitive auto market.

Tesla is becoming the AI powerhouse

As BYD deepens its grip on the EV market, Tesla is pursuing a different direction. While the company is still an EV automaker, investors are increasingly being asked to look beyond its automotive business.

Tesla showed the redesigned Roadster at a SpaceX site near Waco, claiming sub-1-second 0-60 mph, more than 230 mph top speed, and 2028 production, with reservations starting at $50,000.

Rivian said future vehicles will run third-party AI agents and received EPA approval for longer-range 2027 commercial vans with a 129 kWh pack.

GM's Mary Barra defended the exit from Cruise robotaxis while staying on track for eyes-off driving by 2028.

Electric vehicles outpaced consumer imagination this week after giant Tesla Inc (TSLA) finally unveiled its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday with SpaceX thrusters that let the car drive upside down, flip midair, and jump obstacles as high as the company's own Semi truck, while rivals stuck to advancing software, commercial products, and markets.

Tesla Roadster Takes Flight

Tesla on Thursday unveiled the redesigned Roadster at a SpaceX test site near Waco in Texas. The vehicle is developed with technology borrowed from SpaceX, and the display model showed a two-seater interior with a suction system that Musk assured will ease corner maneuvering in addition to helping the car hang upside down, and cold gas thrusters that allow it to flip in the air.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said the car can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in less than one second and reach a top speed of more than 230 mph, with range listed above 300 miles. Musk at the event also termed the car potentially "the only manually driven car Tesla makes," though stunts at the event were performed autonomously. He also said that the vehicle might not be legal in all jurisdictions.

Production for the vehicle, which Musk has previously warned will not move the needle for Tesla financials in a big way, is slated to start in 2028. The company did not disclose a price point for the vehicle, but updated its reservation page to list three variants, including a base version one can reserve for $50,000, a Thrust model which can be reserved for $250,000, and a limited edition Rocket single-seat variant which is invite-only. Tesla said in its reservation agreement that it cannot confirm the purchase price of the vehicle just yet, and reservation holders will know the cost only once they have configured their vehicle order at a later date.

Rivian Pushes AI Agents And Longer-Range Vans

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that future Rivian vehicles will be able to run AI agents from outside companies such as Anthropic, building on the company's own in-car assistant. He described an agentic framework that routes voice requests to local or cloud models depending on complexity. Timing was not given; the company instead pointed to its December AI & Autonomy Day.
